verses.text: Putting away therefore all wickedness, all deceit, hypocrisies, envies, and all evil speaking,
as newborn babies, long for the pure milk of the Word, that with it you may grow,
if indeed you have tasted that the Lord is gracious:
coming to him, a living stone, rejected indeed by men, but chosen by God, precious.
You also, as living stones, are built up as a spiritual house, to be a holy priesthood, to offer up spiritual sacrifices, acceptable to God through Jesus Christ.
Because it is contained in Scripture, “Behold,  I lay in Zion a chief cornerstone, chosen, and precious: He who believes in him will not be disappointed.”
For you who believe therefore is the honor, but for those who are disobedient, “The stone which the builders rejected, has become the chief cornerstone,”
and, “a stone of stumbling, and a rock of offense.”   For they stumble at the word, being disobedient, to which also they were appointed.
But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for God’s own possession, that you may proclaim the excellence of him who called you out of darkness into his marvelous light:
who in time past were no people, but now are God’s people, who had not obtained mercy, but now have obtained mercy.
Beloved, I beg you as foreigners and pilgrims, to abstain from fleshly lusts, which war against the soul;
having good behavior among the nations, so in that of which they speak against you as evildoers, they may by your good works, which they see, glorify God in the day of visitation.
Therefore subject yourselves to every ordinance of man for the Lord’s sake: whether to the king, as supreme;
or to governors, as sent by him for vengeance on evildoers and for praise to those who do well.
For this is the will of God, that by well-doing you should put to silence the ignorance of foolish men:
as free, and not using your freedom for a cloak of wickedness, but as bondservants of God.
Honor all men. Love the brotherhood. Fear God. Honor the king.
Servants, be in subjection to your masters with all fear; not only to the good and gentle, but also to the wicked.
For it is commendable if someone endures pain, suffering unjustly, because of conscience toward God.
For what glory is it if, when you sin, you patiently endure beating? But if, when you do well, you patiently endure suffering, this is commendable with God.
For to this you were called, because Christ also suffered for us, leaving you  an example, that you should follow his steps,
who did not sin, “neither was deceit found in his mouth.”
Who, when he was cursed, didn’t curse back. When he suffered, didn’t threaten, but committed himself to him who judges righteously;
who his own self bore our sins in his body on the tree, that we, having died to sins, might live to righteousness; by whose stripes you were healed.
For you were going astray like sheep; but now have returned to the Shepherd and Overseer  of your souls.

footnotes.content: He tells us to put wickedness away as though it were a soiled garment we could simply remove and set aside. This is no small task, yet the plainness of the instruction gives me hope—it treats us as capable of the act once we've seen it for what it is. Evil speaking, envy, deceit: all habits we can break if Christ has truly changed our heart.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Newborn babes long instinctively for milk; Peter is saying our hunger for God's Word ought to be as natural and urgent. When I've tasted the truth, I find myself wanting more of it—not as duty, but as a child reaching out. Growth comes not by effort alone, but by this honest appetite.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The verse echoes Psalm 34:8. 'Tasted that the Lord is gracious'—what a tender anchor. We don't come to faith by argument first, but by tasting. Once you've known His kindness, even small, you cannot go back to pretending He is harsh or far.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jesus, the living stone—alive, enduring, rejected by the builders of that age yet precious to God. In every century, those who trust the Lord's judgment over the world's have found Him reliable in ways the crowds did not see. He remains solid beneath everything.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: We, too, are living stones, built together into a house of the Spirit. Not dead materials in a heap—alive, each one placed with purpose. The priestly work is spiritual sacrifice: our honest prayer, our small obedience, our yielding of will to His. Offered through Christ, such things are never wasted.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A quotation from Isaiah 28:16. God has already laid the cornerstone in Zion—Christ Himself, chosen and precious. Those who believe in Him find no disappointment because His faithfulness far outlasts our wavering confidence in Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Quoting Psalm 118:22—a stone the builders rejected becomes the chief cornerstone. The great reversal: what the world dismisses, God makes essential. For those who believe, this is honor. For those who refuse Him, it becomes the cause of their stumbling.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Some stumble at the Word because they are disobedient; others become disobedient because they first rejected Him. It's a sobering cycle, yet not beyond God's reach even then. Peter does not soften the truth, but neither does he leave room for despair—grace can reach a stony heart.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Chosen race, royal priesthood, holy nation—these titles once belonged to Israel; now they are ours, grafted in through Christ. What an elevation for people once far from God. He has called us from darkness into light so we might tell of His excellence. That calling is both privilege and responsibility.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: There was a time we were no people, outside His covenant, having no mercy. Now we are His people, having found mercy. This transformation is not earned by our merit but received as a gift. The wonder of it deserves our lifelong gratitude and our loyalty.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He calls us 'foreigners and pilgrims'—we don't belong to this world's system. Lusts of the flesh war against the soul like an invading army. Peter isn't saying the body is evil, but that yielding to its base desires breaks peace within us. He asks us to recognize we are pilgrims passing through.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Good behavior among the nations speaks louder than any word we could say. Those who slander us may eventually see in our deeds the hand of God and glorify Him on 'the day of visitation'—when His judgment comes or His grace is finally seen. Our conduct is a silent witness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Submit to earthly authority for the Lord's sake. This doesn't mean every law is just, but that rebellion and disorder are not our way. We obey Christ by honoring the order He permits, even when rulers are flawed. It is an act of faith in His sovereignty.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Governors are sent by God to punish evildoers and praise those who do well. This is the ideal: civil order that rewards righteousness. We live in that reality imperfectly, yet Peter reminds us that good rule reflects God's will. Our task is to do well and trust His purposes.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Well-doing silences the ignorant accusations of foolish men. There is power in simply living a holy life while others rage. It is God's will that our goodness become the answer to their slander. We fight not with words but with faithful conduct.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: As free—yes, Christ has set us free—yet not free to use freedom as a cloak for wickedness. True freedom is not the absence of law but the joy of serving God willingly. We are His bondservants, and in that service we find the deepest liberty.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Four imperatives in one verse, crystalline and plain: honor all men, love the brothers and sisters in Christ, fear God (the root of all wisdom), honor the king. A summary of how to live—upright, loving, reverent, and loyal.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Even to wicked masters, servants are called to subjection with fear. This is a hard word, yet it reveals a truth: our obedience to the Lord does not depend on the worthiness of earthly authorities. We serve Christ through every role, every circumstance.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: To endure unjust suffering for conscience sake—to suffer not because you deserve it, but because you've chosen to obey God rather than men—this is commendable. Peter dignifies it: there is honor in it, not shame. Conscience toward God outweighs the cost.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: There is no glory in patiently bearing a beating you earned by your own sin. But to endure pain while doing well—that speaks of a strength not of this world. God sees such patient innocence and counts it commendable. The world may scoff, but He marks it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Christ suffered for us and left us an example. He didn't merely suffer on our behalf; He showed us how to walk in suffering—faithfully, without bitterness, toward His Father's purposes. We are called to follow His steps, not to walk them alone.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A quotation from Isaiah 53:9. Christ was without sin, and no deceit was found in His mouth. His suffering was not the payment for His own wrongs but the bearing of ours. In Him, innocence itself walked into injustice and triumphed by staying true.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When cursed, He did not curse back; when suffering, He did not threaten. Instead, He committed Himself to the One who judges justly. This is the hardest step of all: to lay down the right to retaliate and entrust your vindication to God. Yet it is the path to peace.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Christ bore our sins in His body on the tree—a cost beyond measure. We, having died to sin through His work, are now freed to live to righteousness. 'By His stripes you were healed' speaks not only of spiritual restoration but of the price He paid so we could be whole.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo: we were wandering like lost sheep, and the Shepherd has brought us home. Even now, in a world of noise and distraction, He watches over the souls He has called His own. The metaphor is old, yet the tender care it speaks of is as present as morning light.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
